system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2118-07-18 17:20:00 to 2118-07-21 16:32:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a thrombosed left upper extremity AV graft, preventing dialysis. She also reported persistent abdominal nodules at insulin injection sites and chronic urinary symptoms. Imaging confirmed bladder wall enhancement suggestive of infection and a non-specific lytic lesion in L1, but no abscesses or calciphylaxis. The AV graft was successfully recanalized via thrombectomy. Wound culture from a prior breast biopsy grew pan-sensitive E. coli and Proteus, treated with targeted IV ceftazidime. Urine culture was contaminated, but symptoms improved with empiric antibiotics. She completed one dialysis session during admission and was transitioned to outpatient IV antibiotic administration post-dialysis. Discharged home with services, on a plan for continued dialysis, wound care, and close follow-up for unresolved abdominal nodules and repeat urine testing if symptoms persist.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Proteus (mirabilis) (morganii) infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ lady with end-stage renal disease with left upper arm AV
graft, which now presents thrombosed.  Patient underwent prior percutaneous
thrombectomies of this AV graft in ___ and in ___.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ and Dr. ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Informed consent was obtained from the patient.  The patient was
placed supine on the angiography table.  The left upper extremity was prepped
and draped in a standard sterile fashion.  A preprocedural timeout was
performed.  After administration of 10 mL of lidocaine 1%, access was gained
into the left upper arm AV graft in the antegrade and retrograde directions
using micropuncture sheaths followed by 6 ___ sheaths.  A pullback venogram
was obtained, which demonstrated thrombus extending from the graft all the way
to the axillary vein.  Then, spraying of the thrombus in the outflow vein, as
well as in the entire length of the graft was performed using the AngioJet
device.  A total of 12 mg of tPA were sprayed throughout the length of the
thrombus.

Then, percutaneous thrombectomy was performed in the outflow vein and
throughout the entire length of the graft using the AngioJet device.  This was
followed by balloon maceration of any residual clot using a 7 mm balloon.  A
___ embolectomy catheter was then used to remove the arterial plug across
the arterial anastomosis.  Flow was then restored through the graft and a
fistulogram was obtained.  It demonstrated residual stenosis in the arterial
limb of the graft and inflow stenosis at the arterial anastomotic site.

Then, the arterial anastomosis and inflow artery were dilated using a 4 mm
angioplasty balloon.  A residual waist was seen on the balloon.  Then, the
arterial anastomotic site was dilated with a 5 mm balloon to its maximum
pressure with still a residual waist remaining.  A followup retrograde
injection into the brachial artery demonstrated residual arterial anastomotic
stenosis.  Then, angioplasty of the arterial limb of the graft was performed
using a 6- and a 7-mm balloon and again in this area a residual waist
indicating persistent stenosis was seen even after angioplasty to 20
atmospheres.  During angioplasty of the arterial limb of the graft, there was
rupture of the angioplasty balloon.  Retrieval of the angioplasty balloon
through the access sheath was not possible; therefore, using the opposite
direction sheath, a snare device was used to retrieve the angioplasty balloon.

At this stage re-thrombosis of the graft was noticed based on the persistent
and refractory to high-pressure angioplasty stenotic lesions both in the
arterial anastomosis/inflow as well as in the arterial limb of the graft.  We
discussed these findings with the surgical team and a plan was made for
possible surgical revision of these areas refractory to high-pressure balloon
angioplasty.

Then, attention was directed towards placement of a hemodialysis catheter. 
Both sides of the neck were prepped and draped in a standard sterile fashion. 
Access was obtained into the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound
guidance.  However, a guidewire would not progress and contrast injection
demonstrated occlusion of this vein.  Then, attention was directed towards the
left internal jugular vein.  Needle access was obtained and a 0.018 guidewire
was advanced into the right atrium.  The access was dilated using a
micropuncture sheath and sequential 12- and ___ dilators.  A temporary
dialysis catheter was placed under fluoroscopic guidance, due to the patient's
discomfort from being on the procedure table for so long.  The catheter was
flushed and secured to the skin with 0 silk sutures.  Caps were placed, a
sterile dressing was applied.  Catheter tip is located in the right atrium as
confirmed by a spot fluoroscopic image saved.  Hard copies of ultrasound
images were obtained before and after establishing venous access into the left
internal jugular vein and images demonstrate vein patency before and after.

COMPLICATIONS:  Rupture of angioplasty balloon during angioplasty of the
arterial limb of the graft, with successful retrieval of the ruptured balloon.

MEDICATIONS:  TPA 12 mg, hydralazine 60 mg, fentanyl 300 mcg, Versed 5 mg. 
Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of Versed and
fentanyl through a total intraservice time of 3 hours and 30 minutes.  The
vital signs were continuously monitored by an independently trained radiology
nurse, during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Unsuccessful thrombectomy and angioplasty of a left upper arm AV graft due
to presence of persistent stenosis in the arterial anastomosis as well as
arterial limb of the graft refractory to high-pressure angioplasty.
2.  Central veins and outflow of the graft, including previously stented
segments were recanalized without difficulty.
3.  Placement of a temporary hemodialysis catheter via the left internal
jugular vein.  Patient may return to Interventional Radiology, if appropriate,
for conversion to tunneled dialysis catheter.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  Hemodialysis, preoperative assessment.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  As compared to the previous radiograph, the patient has received a
hemodialysis catheter over the left central venous access.  The sternal wires
are in unchanged alignment.  Status post CABG.  No evidence of pneumothorax. 
Moderate cardiomegaly with signs of mild fluid overload but no overt pulmonary
edema.  Low lung volumes with atelectasis in the retrocardiac lung region.  No
pleural effusions.

HISTORY:  Abdominal wound. ? Abscess around abdominal wound. 

COMPARISON :

CT dated ___.  

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale ultrasound images of the anterior abdominal wall were
obtained.  

FINDINGS:

In the region of concern in the left lower quadrant, no fluid collection is
identified.  There is also no subcutaneous fluid collection within the right
lower quadrant.  

IMPRESSION:

No fluid collection.

INDICATION:  End-stage renal disease.  Place tunneled hemodialysis line.

COMPARISONS:  AV fistulogram from ___.  AV fistulogram from
___.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___, Dr. ___, and Dr. ___
(___).  Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the
procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was performed by administering divided doses of
100 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed during a total in-service time of 15
minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were monitored by an
independent radiology nurse.  Local anesthesia was provided with 1% lidocaine
and 1% lidocaine with epi along the tunneling tract.

CONTRAST:  None.

FLUOROSCOPY:  Total time 2.3 minutes; total dose 13 mGy.

PROCEDURE:  Tunneled dialysis catheter placement.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:  Informed, written consent was obtained after explaining
the procedures, benefits, alternatives, and risks involved.  The patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed in the supine position on the
imaging table.  The left neck was prepped and draped in the usual sterile
fashion, including the temporary hemodialysis line which was present in the
left internal jugular vein.  A preprocedure timeout was performed per the
___ protocol.

A ___ wire was placed through the existing temporary left internal jugular
catheter.  The measurement was obtained for the wire and a 28 cm hemodialysis
line was selected.

The direction of the tunnel was determined and the tunnel tract was
anesthetized with lidocaine with epinephrine.  The catheter was tunneled
underneath the skin.  The existing temporary right internal jugular catheter
was removed over the wire.  A right internal jugular vein sheath was placed at
the site of the existing temporary catheter.  The new catheter was placed
through this sheath and the peel-away sheath was removed.  The tip was found
to be in the right atrium.  Final fluoroscopic images demonstrate the tip in
the right atrium.  There is normal blood return from both lumens.  The
catheter was flushed.

The catheter was secured to the skin using silk sutures.  The venotomy site
was closed with a subcutaneous stitch.  The patient left the department in
stable condition.  She tolerated the procedure well.  No immediate
complications were identified.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated conversion of a left temporary hemodialysis
catheter to a tunneled hemodialysis catheter.  The tip is in the right atrium.
The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your dialysis access wasn’t working today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The nurses at dialysis tried to use my arm graft, but couldn’t get it to work. I’ve had this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you were here about a month ago for the same issue. We’ll need to check your graft again. How are you feeling otherwise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. No chest pain, no shortness of breath. Just worried I can’t get dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll make sure you get dialysis while you’re here. First, we’ll do some blood work and get you set up for a procedure tomorrow to look at your graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they try to fix it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the transplant surgery team will do a fistulogram and try to clear the clot. But sometimes, if it’s blocked too much, we may need a temporary catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a catheter once before. I didn’t like it in my neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We only use it temporarily. It helps us keep your dialysis on schedule while your arm graft heals or gets repaired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s not forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You just came back from the procedure. The team tried to open up your graft, but there was a tough blockage they couldn’t fully clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it didn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely. They opened part of it, but there’s still a narrow spot that didn’t respond to the balloon. Because of that, they decided to place a temporary catheter in your neck for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very common. We’ll make sure it’s clean and monitored. You’ll get dialysis through it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my arm? Will they try again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgeons recommend an outpatient procedure to repair the graft. They’ll contact you to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Your kidney numbers are improving after dialysis. We’ll keep an eye on your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic before. Is that still a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is lower than ideal, but it’s expected with kidney disease. You’re on erythropoietin, which helps. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your abdominal wound yesterday. Good news — no abscess or fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still tender. Should I keep cleaning it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The wound care team recommends cleaning it with a wound cleanser, applying DuoDerm gel, and covering it with a Mepilex dressing every three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? I was on ceftazidime before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since there’s no sign of active infection, we’re not continuing IV antibiotics. But you’ll keep the wound care at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my breast wound? It’s still packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That wound is healing. We’ll keep packing it daily. You should follow up with the breast clinic as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update — we’ve replaced the temporary catheter in your neck with a tunneled one. It’s more secure and meant for longer use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a better version — same spot, but it goes under the skin and is less likely to get infected or move out of place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your regular dialysis schedule using the catheter in your neck. The transplant team will contact you to fix your arm graft as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse come to help with both wounds. They’ll follow the same cleaning and dressing routine we’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I won’t be alone with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send your medications home with you. Most are the same, including your insulin, heart meds, and pain patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re stopping those. The wounds aren’t infected now, so we don’t need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your daughter gets a call with the discharge details. You’ll be going home with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’ll be relieved. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was re-admitted due to a thrombosed left upper extremity AV graft, preventing dialysis access. A fistulogram and thrombectomy were attempted but were unsuccessful due to persistent stenosis in the graft. A temporary dialysis catheter was placed in the left internal jugular vein and later converted to a tunneled catheter. The patient received one dialysis session during admission and was stabilized. Chronic abdominal and left breast wounds were assessed; no abscess was found, and wound care was optimized for home management. The transplant surgery team will contact the patient to schedule outpatient graft repair. She was discharged home with visiting nurse services for wound care and instructions to resume regular dialysis through the tunneled catheter.
